video_title: The AI Gold Rush Meets an Oil Shock | Protect the Pile Episode 25
gist: Hedgeye's portfolio managers argue oil-driven inflation (Iran sanctions, Houthi Red Sea blockade, draining SPR/private inventories) could keep the US in a string of Quad 2 (growth+inflation accelerating) macro regimes through the midterms, while a separate debate breaks out over whether AI capex is a self-funding bubble given hyperscaler cash burn, price wars between OpenAI/Anthropic/Meta, and wildly inflated TAM claims — with data-layer names like Snowflake, Databricks and Palantir flagged as safer plays than the model labs themselves.

themes.theme: Macro regime: Quad 2 persistence, dollar, and Fed independence

insights.claim: With oil trading around $92 (above Hedgeye's risk-range low of $86) and both growth and inflation data accelerating, the panel sees rising odds of the US economy running a string of consecutive 'Quad 2' (rising growth, rising inflation) months through September, October, and possibly November, which has direct sector allocation implications (broad risk-on, low-quality/high-beta outperformance, financials strength).
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK, host)
insights.so_what: A confirmed Quad 2 stretch argues for staying overweight cyclicals, financials, and high-beta/low-quality risk assets rather than defensives, while watching oil and the dollar as the swing factors that could flip the regime to Quad 1.
insights.quote: we're looking like with growth and inflation both accelerating and now the monthly looks like the monthly cods are starting to converge so that we could be on a string of like this month o September October and I guess maybe possibly November um all quad 2

insights.claim: The single biggest swing factor determining whether the macro regime rotates from Quad 2 to Quad 1 is the path of oil prices, since an escalation or ceasefire headline could flip the inflation/growth mix quickly.
insights.speaker: Sam (Sam Ramen)
insights.so_what: Traders using the Hedgeye quad framework should treat oil headlines (Iran, Russia, Venezuela) as the primary catalyst risk for a regime-change trade in sector rotation.
insights.quote: I think that the key determining factor between those two is going to be what happens to oil

insights.claim: New Fed chair Kevin Warsh gave a more hawkish-than-expected speech at Jackson Hole, abandoning traditional forward guidance and effectively telling markets to figure out the rate path themselves — a move interpreted as Warsh asserting independence from both market expectations and, implicitly, from Trump/Treasury pressure for lower rates.
insights.speaker: Neil Howe
insights.so_what: A hawkish, independent-minded Fed chair reduces the probability of imminent rate cuts even amid administration pressure for a weaker dollar — bond and dollar positioning should not assume political capture of the Fed.
insights.quote: it was amazingly, you know, I mean I should say hawkish... it's remarkable too, you know, having giving up all for all forward guidance

insights.claim: The panel frames the Trump administration's broader strategy as a 'political business cycle' explicitly oriented around getting through the midterms — including deliberately delaying a major defense budget increase (from roughly $200-300B in current appropriations toward a targeted $1.5 trillion total) until after the midterms via a lame-duck reconciliation push, rather than pursuing 'permanent solutions' now.
insights.speaker: Neil Howe
insights.so_what: Defense contractors (e.g., RTX) may continue to underperform their promised order books near-term because actual appropriations for the larger $1.5T defense buildout are being deferred until after the midterms — a timing consideration for defense-sector positioning.
insights.quote: all of that's going to be done after the midterms before the new Congress comes in... this is going to completely transform defense spending

insights.claim: Currently RTX and other defense primes are 'promising a lot' but not delivering much revenue growth because new defense appropriations are stuck behind partisan budget gridlock, meaning current defense stock re-rating is running ahead of actual funded backlog.
insights.speaker: Neil Howe / Sam
insights.so_what: Watch for the post-midterm reconciliation bill as the actual catalyst for defense-sector earnings realization; current valuations may be pricing in appropriations that haven't yet been approved.
insights.quote: this is why RTX and those companies aren't really doing a lot. They're promising a lot. They're not doing a lot because no one can come up with the money. That's because we got a partisan gridlock

insights.claim: The administration wants a weaker dollar across the board (to ease debt/trade dynamics), but the panel frames this as a tug-of-war the market may not concede, especially since a weaker dollar right now would exacerbate inflation and complicate the Fed's independent stance.
insights.speaker: Sam / Patrick Kent
insights.so_what: Dollar bears should watch whether Fed independence (under Warsh) holds against administration pressure — a genuinely independent, hawkish Fed is a headwind to the administration's weak-dollar policy goal and a support for the dollar near-term.
insights.quote: this administration across the board wants a week dollar. Now the question is will the market give it to them and that is I think the big tug of war

insights.claim: Hedgeye's proprietary global dollar liquidity measure had been improving toward 'green light' levels roughly a week before recording but reversed back down (toward a ~4% growth 'yellow light' threshold) after Warsh's hawkish comments strengthened the dollar, correlating with a pickup in VIX and large-cap outperformance over small caps.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK, host)
insights.so_what: Global dollar liquidity is a real-time cross-asset signal the panel actively uses to anticipate risk-on/risk-off rotations between large vs small cap and volatility regime changes — worth tracking as a leading indicator alongside Fed rhetoric.
insights.quote: my liquidity measures will pick right back up you know they were all starting to go green lights just like a week or so ago and then this strengthening in the dollar after Wars' comments kind of pulled them back in

themes.theme: Oil shock: Iran, Houthis, and depleting strategic reserves

insights.claim: The Houthis have effectively closed off the Bab-el-Mandeb strait (the southern end of the Red Sea), forcing Saudi Arabia and other shippers to reroute via a costly overland truck route from Iraq through Syria, which raises effective shipping costs and increases oil held in transit inventory even as onshore stockpiles (including the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve) continue to decline.
insights.speaker: Neil Howe
insights.so_what: Physical shipping disruption is now compounding, not just threatening, oil supply — rising day-sales-of-inventory in transit plus falling SPR and (poorly measured) private refined-product inventories argue for a structurally higher oil price floor, not just headline-driven spikes.
insights.quote: they basically closed off the bubble mandab... Saudi Arabia is no longer using that. And that that is actually pinching off a lot of what used to be running

insights.claim: There is no reliable public data on private inventories of refined petroleum products (as opposed to crude), and the panel suspects those inventories may be falling faster than realized as market participants sell down stock now on the belief the war/sanctions won't last, creating hidden downside inventory risk ('empty shelves').
insights.speaker: Neil Howe
insights.so_what: A blind spot in refined-product inventory data means an oil/gasoline price spike could arrive with less warning than crude-only data suggests — worth monitoring physical indicators like Cushing tank photos as an alternative signal.
insights.quote: we know least is that the private inventories of refined products there is no record of that right and it may be that the that those inventories are really going down

insights.claim: US missile interceptor inventories are severely depleted (partly from prior transfers to Ukraine and prior Houthi strikes), and because interceptors are inherently and permanently more expensive than the offensive missiles/drones they counter, the panel argues the only durable long-term solution to threats like the Houthis and Iran is ground invasion — a course no one currently wants to pursue given the cost and casualties.
insights.speaker: Neil Howe
insights.so_what: Structural interceptor-cost asymmetry means missile-defense-dependent strategies against Iran/Houthis are financially unsustainable long-term, implying prolonged, unresolved regional conflict and sustained oil-supply risk premium rather than a quick military resolution.
insights.quote: the whole history of missile anti-missile warfare is that the interceptors are always more expensive, much more expensive... to finish that off, you've got to go in on the ground

insights.claim: Roughly a third of Iran's current external support/supply is arriving via the Caspian Sea, with China and Russia reportedly actively supplying Iran with technology, food, and rocket fuel despite Trump's claim that Putin personally assured him Russia was not selling anything to Iran.
insights.speaker: Neil Howe
insights.so_what: Active Russia/China material support for Iran undermines the effectiveness of US sanctions and implies the Iran conflict (and its oil-market impact) is unlikely to de-escalate quickly, reinforcing a higher-for-longer oil risk premium thesis.
insights.quote: China and Russia are actively supporting Iran. They're giving them technology. They're giving them food. They're giving them rocket fuel. This is like an active support effort.

insights.claim: The panel views proposed US/Chevron plans to restore Venezuelan oil production (from under 1.5 million barrels/day back toward its historical ~3 million bpd peak) as mostly rhetorical ('smoke and mirrors') in the near-to-medium term, since it would require billions in fixed investment, faces legal obstacles on both the Pentagon and Venezuelan constitutional sides, and depends on sustained high oil prices and a stable regime that doesn't yet exist.
insights.speaker: Brooks Cutright / Neil Howe
insights.so_what: Don't treat Venezuela supply-restoration headlines as a near-term bearish catalyst for oil prices; the actual capacity increase is likely years away and contingent on legal/political resolution — Chevron's public commitments carry little near-term cost to make and shouldn't be read as imminent supply relief.
insights.quote: it costs me nothing as Chevron to get on the tape and be like we will absolutely spend billions to bring back up production in Venezuela... no one's going to start doing this right now

insights.claim: The most recent leg up in oil/gas prices is attributed less to Iran alone (where oil is reportedly still 'seeping through' Hormuz and other channels) and more to rising concern about Russia's response to Ukrainian refinery strikes and potential Russian escalation (including possible false-flag operations in the Baltics), evidenced by European natural gas prices breaking out and US Henry Hub gas prices also trending higher into the fall/winter.
insights.speaker: Sam (Sam Ramen)
insights.so_what: European and US natural gas prices breaking into bullish trend are a tell that markets are now pricing a broader Russia-Ukraine energy-infrastructure conflict, not just an Iran risk premium — relevant for positioning in natural gas and European utility/energy exposure heading into winter.
insights.quote: European gas prices and look at look at Henry Hub gas prices here. They've started to sort of creep higher particularly in Europe. They're they're they're flat out breaking out

insights.claim: The panel is skeptical of claims that falling oil demand (due to lower consumption) explains the muted price response to the Iran conflict, noting US and European airline/fuel usage is actually higher this summer than last summer; they suspect the more likely explanation is inventory drawdown as holders sell existing stock now on the bet that prices will fall once the conflict ends.
insights.speaker: Neil Howe
insights.so_what: If the demand-destruction narrative is wrong and inventory drawdown is the real driver, current oil prices may understate the true supply tightness, raising the risk of a sharper price spike once visible inventories (e.g., Cushing) run critically low.
insights.quote: I don't see many major airlines around the world cutting back usage. In fact, in the United States and Europe, usage is higher this summer than last summer. I don't see it.

themes.theme: AI capex: cash burn, price wars, and inflated TAM claims

insights.claim: The AI buildout is described as the single most consequential force in current US real economic activity, but it is being funded by extremely loose capital even though none of the major AI labs or hyperscalers are generating positive cash flow — they are burning cash at an accelerating rate, which the panel argues means intelligence/compute is not showing the return-on-invested-capital dynamics that 'electricity' analogies imply.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK, host)
insights.so_what: The AI capex boom is currently a financing-dependent phenomenon rather than a self-funding one; any tightening in credit/funding conditions (rising 10-year yields, tighter capital markets) is a direct risk to the pace of AI infrastructure buildout.
insights.quote: none of the certainly none of the AI companies are generating cash flow right they are burning cash at an extremely high rate... if intelligence is the new electricity that does not bode well for returns on invested capital

insights.claim: A model-quality 'horse race' dynamic (Meta's new model release, OpenAI and Google responding) is forcing every major AI lab to keep investing aggressively just to avoid falling behind in rankings, while several labs are simultaneously cutting consumer prices (Meta, OpenAI) — the panelist argues this combination is actually destructive to capital efficiency because it juices near-term demand on existing (non-improving) GPU capital stock (A100s/H100s) rather than allowing efficiency gains to compound.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK, host)
insights.so_what: Price cuts aimed at winning the model-usage horse race may be capital-destructive rather than efficiency-driven — a red flag for AI infrastructure investors expecting hardware efficiency gains to offset falling per-token pricing.
insights.quote: the more you juice this demand in the near term, the less that efficiency comes down because you're lighting everything... you're actually kind of destroying more capital and it's going to be even more dependent on the funding environment

insights.claim: A counter-view from another panelist holds that Anthropic's newest model ('Fable 5.1') achieved much of its impressiveness through algorithmic efficiency gains that substantially lowered cost-per-token without materially sacrificing token generation speed, and predicts Anthropic could show actual trailing six-month operating profit and software-like gross margins when its next funding round/S-1 materializes.
insights.speaker: Sam (Sam Ramen)
insights.so_what: A specific, checkable prediction: watch Anthropic's next disclosure (S-1 or funding round materials) for evidence of software-like gross margins and possible profitability — if true, it would validate the efficiency-improvement bull case against the cash-burn bear case for AI labs.
insights.quote: I would not be surprised if we see software like gross margins for that company and maybe on a trailing six-month basis... an actual operating profit for anthropic

insights.claim: The panel dismisses widely circulated AI industry revenue TAM figures (e.g., a rumored ~$30 trillion figure and OpenAI figures around $35 trillion, allegedly floated to top SpaceX's ~$285B valuation narrative) as essentially made-up numbers with no analytical basis, comparable to citing global GDP.
insights.speaker: Sam (Sam Ramen) / Patrick Kent
insights.so_what: Investors should heavily discount headline AI TAM figures used to justify valuations; they function as narrative marketing rather than grounded forecasts.
insights.quote: these are all just madeup numbers at this point... it's laughable the number's laughable but really it's irrelevant

insights.claim: Breaking down Jensen Huang's claim of $400B invested in AI startups over the last 6 months: roughly $200B of that is OpenAI and Anthropic themselves, and of the remaining ~$200B in other AI startups, an estimated ~50% is being spent buying AI compute/data center rental capacity from the hyperscalers — meaning a large share of 'AI startup revenue' is circular spending with no associated profit, since these are by definition early-stage companies where the VC base-rate implies ~90% will fail.
insights.speaker: Sam (Sam Ramen)
insights.so_what: A meaningful share of headline AI investment figures represents circular, non-durable revenue (startups paying hyperscalers for compute) rather than end-market demand — near-term AI infrastructure demand is likely overstated once startup failure rates are applied.
insights.quote: there's a 100red billion of revenue coming through here that has no profit associated with it... we are probably overstating the demand for this in the near term. Full stop.

insights.claim: Drawing an explicit analogy to the dot-com boom, the panel argues AI has not yet reached its 'eBay/Priceline/Amazon' inflection point — the moment when genuinely transformative consumer/enterprise applications emerge — and notes that those 1990s companies only reached that maturity after a crash; the implication is current AI infrastructure investment could similarly be ahead of its real application demand curve and vulnerable to a similar boom-bust pattern.
insights.speaker: Sam (Sam Ramen)
insights.so_what: History-informed base rate: infrastructure/valuation booms in transformative technology typically precede (and can be followed by a crash before) the real application-driven demand phase — a caution against assuming current AI infrastructure spending is proportionate to durable end demand.
insights.quote: The real application inflection point scurve was when you got companies like eBay, Priceeline.com, Amazon... We have yet to get to that point.

insights.claim: Corporate/enterprise AI usage data shows an extreme, more-than-80/20 bifurcation: only about 1-2% of users (largely enterprise/software engineers) reportedly drive over 90% of total token consumption at both Anthropic and OpenAI, meaning current AI monetization is highly concentrated in a narrow power-user base rather than broad-based consumer adoption.
insights.speaker: Sam (Sam Ramen)
insights.so_what: Mass-market consumer AI monetization ('mom and pop' usage) has not yet materialized at scale; investors betting on AI's TAM should distinguish between enterprise/developer-driven revenue (already large) and the much smaller, still-nascent broad consumer usage base.
insights.quote: 1% or 2% of users of uh both anthropic and openi and you can imagine that probably mostly enterprise users use like over 90%... this massive bifocation where the earliest adopters, the extreme users, the software engineers are driving the vast majority of the token consumption

insights.claim: Independent (non-industry) survey data on actual out-of-pocket enterprise spending on AI outside the tech/financial sectors reportedly comes in surprisingly low, cited around $30-40 billion, which one panelist argues needs to scale up considerably to justify the current multi-hundred-billion-dollar AI investment pyramid.
insights.speaker: Neil Howe
insights.so_what: A specific, trackable figure (~$30-40B in real-world non-tech enterprise AI spend) to benchmark against future surveys — if this figure fails to grow rapidly, it would support the bear case that AI infrastructure investment is running far ahead of monetizable demand.
insights.quote: I saw one one survey which actually attempted a number and it was something like you know 30 40 billion dollars

themes.theme: AI competitive dynamics: winners beyond the model labs

insights.claim: Anthropic reportedly enabled its flagship model ('Fable 5.1') for typical corporate accounts (previously restricted mostly to a retail/individual tier, capped at an estimated 15-20% of usage share on internal histograms) on a metered, pay-per-token basis rather than flat-fee, which one panelist interprets as a deliberate short-term margin/usage-juicing move timed ahead of a fundraising roadshow, likening it to a 'teaser rate' unlikely to retain sticky usage once initial projects are complete.
insights.speaker: Brooks Cutright
insights.so_what: Near-term usage/revenue spikes tied to promotional or teaser-rate access to premium AI models should be discounted as durable demand signals, particularly ahead of a company's fundraising events.
insights.quote: they're trying to juice Babel and high-end and effectively margin in the next like week or two by rolling this out and making it available in time to show people how useful it is as they go... on their road show

insights.claim: A practitioner-level workflow insight: using two different AI models to cross-check and audit each other's output (e.g., generating with Claude and then having Codex audit it) produces dramatically better hallucination/error-rate reduction (~80% fewer errors for roughly 2x the cost) than repeatedly querying the same model or having a single model self-check, because a model reviewing its own or a 'twin's' work is inherently sycophantic.
insights.speaker: Brooks Cutright
insights.so_what: For any team building AI-driven research/analysis workflows, cross-model adversarial auditing (rather than single-model or same-model self-review) is a concrete, cost-effective way to materially cut hallucination risk — a practical edge for investment research operations using LLMs.
insights.quote: you get way more bang for my buck in in terms of managing hallucinations and error rates by having a confluence of Claude and Codeex effectively talking to each other... you're cutting your error rates down by like 80%

insights.claim: The panel argues that 'orchestration layer' and enterprise data platform companies — specifically Snowflake, Databricks, and Palantir — are structurally well-positioned to benefit from AI regardless of which model wins, because enterprises want to avoid full lock-in to a single cloud provider or model vendor, prefer to keep proprietary data walled off from any single AI lab (e.g., not wanting to hand it all to Anthropic), and want to price-shop across open- and closed-weight models for different tasks.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK, host) / Sam (Sam Ramen)
insights.so_what: A concrete pairs/basket idea: favor multi-cloud, model-agnostic data/orchestration platforms (Snowflake, Databricks, Palantir) over single model-lab exposure as a way to capture AI monetization while avoiding the cash-burn and price-war risk concentrated at the foundation-model layer; Databricks' upcoming IPO/S-1 flagged as a name to watch closely.
insights.quote: these data layers at least for a little while actually are the ones that might be in the best position... especially if enterprises want to retain control of their proprietary data

insights.claim: Data/orchestration platforms like Snowflake are described as having a more favorable structural position than pure hyperscalers because they profit from data query/agent volume regardless of whether that volume translates to end-customer profitability, whereas hyperscalers are 'long quantity' of data and compute usage — the panel notes Snowflake's recent quarter beat and stronger-than-expected forward guidance as early evidence of this dynamic playing out, attributing it to agentic AI layers driving increased querying of enterprises' own data.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK, host)
insights.so_what: Snowflake's outsized quarterly beat/guide is cited as live confirmation of the data-layer thesis — a data point worth tracking in subsequent Snowflake, Databricks, and Palantir earnings for continuation or reversal of the trend.
insights.quote: already we can see it in the acceleration they put up in this quarter they shocked me with what they guided to for the next quarter... I think that as that agent layer is taking off they're getting paid on like pinging your own data

insights.claim: Apple is flagged as a company uniquely positioned to benefit from AI applications due to its distribution advantage (over a billion device users) despite having no leading in-house AI model, having already partnered with Google/Gemini to bring AI functionality to iPhones expected within the next few months, though the panel is skeptical about whether Siri-based AI will actually be compelling.
insights.speaker: Neil Howe / Patrick Kent
insights.so_what: Apple's massive distribution reach makes it a candidate 'killer app' vector for consumer AI even without owning frontier model IP — watch the Google-Gemini-powered Siri upgrade rollout (expected within months per company timeline) as a potential catalyst for broad consumer AI adoption.
insights.quote: they have the distribution... a billion plus users... they're already working with Google on Gemini to bring AI functionality to the phone. We have yet to see it.
